title: Prepaid Electricity in Texas: Pros, Cons & Costs (2026)
h1: Prepaid electricity in Texas: how it works, pros, cons and real costs
desc: Prepaid electricity in Texas skips the deposit and credit check, but daily balance tracking means disconnection risk. See how it compares to postpaid plans.
lede: Prepaid electricity in Texas lets you pay for power before you use it, usually with no deposit and no credit check. You load funds onto an account, track your balance daily, and add money as needed. The tradeoff is that running out of funds can lead to same-day disconnection, so it suits people who want control, not long contracts.
body:
What prepaid electricity in Texas actually means

Prepaid electricity flips the normal billing order. Instead of using power for a month and getting a bill afterward, you add funds to an account upfront, and your usage draws down that balance in near real time. Texas is a deregulated electricity market, which is why dozens of retail electric providers (REPs) offer prepaid plans alongside traditional postpaid ones.

Your smart meter reports usage daily, so your provider can update your balance every day instead of waiting for a monthly read. You can usually check your balance through an app, text alerts, or an online portal at any hour.

No deposit, no credit check: why people choose prepaid

The single biggest reason renters and homeowners pick prepaid electricity is that it typically requires no security deposit and no credit check. Postpaid plans in Texas can require a deposit of up to the greater of one-fifth of your estimated annual billing or two estimated monthly bills, unless you qualify for a waiver (for example, if you're 65 or older with no delinquent history, a certified family violence victim, or you can show a satisfactory payment history letter from a previous provider).

Prepaid plans sidestep that entirely because the provider is never extending you credit. You're always paying ahead of your usage, so there's little default risk for them to price into a deposit. If a deposit is the main thing standing between you and getting power turned on, it's worth reading our guide on Texas electricity with no deposit, which covers prepaid plans and three other legal ways to skip the deposit.

Daily balance alerts and how disconnection works

Because prepaid accounts are funded in advance, providers lean heavily on daily balance alerts to keep you from running dry. Most prepaid plans let you set a low-balance threshold, commonly somewhere around $10 to $25, and will text or email you when your balance drops below it.

The catch is speed. On a postpaid plan, falling behind triggers a billing cycle, a due date, and often a grace period before disconnection. On a prepaid plan, your balance can hit zero in the middle of a hot afternoon, and some providers can disconnect service the same day, sometimes even on weekends, depending on their terms. That's the core tradeoff: no deposit and more control over cash flow, in exchange for a shorter runway if you forget to add funds.

A quick math check on how fast a balance can disappear

Here's a worked example using real Texas delivery charges so you can see how quickly a low balance can run out during a high-usage month.

Say your prepaid plan charges an energy rate of 14 cents per kWh, and your home is served by Oncor Electric Delivery (the largest Texas utility for delivery purposes). In August, your home uses 1,500 kWh, which is typical for a Texas house running central air conditioning hard.

  • Energy charge: 1,500 kWh × $0.14 = $210.00
  • Oncor delivery charge: $4.23 fixed + (1,500 kWh × $0.06013) = $4.23 + $90.20 = $94.43
  • Total cost for the month: $210.00 + $94.43 = $304.43
  • Effective average price: $304.43 ÷ 1,500 kWh = about 20.3 cents per kWh
  • Average daily cost: $304.43 ÷ 31 days = about $9.82 per day

If you start August with a $50 balance and don't add funds, you'll run dry in roughly 5 days ($50 ÷ $9.82 ≈ 5.1 days). That's why prepaid customers who do well tend to check their balance at least every few days during peak summer and winter months, not just when an alert arrives.

Prepaid vs. postpaid electricity rates in Texas

Prepaid and postpaid plans both have to publish an Electricity Facts Label (EFL) showing average price per kWh at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 kWh of usage, so the rate itself isn't automatically higher or lower just because a plan is prepaid. What differs is the fee structure and billing rhythm. Here's how the two models typically compare.

FeaturePrepaid electricityPostpaid electricity
Deposit requiredUsually noneOften required unless you qualify for a waiver
Credit checkUsually noneCommon, especially for new customers
Billing cyclePay-ahead, balance updates dailyMonthly bill after usage
Contract lengthOften month-to-monthOften 6 to 36 month fixed terms
Disconnection riskCan happen quickly once balance hits zeroFollows a billing and grace-period process
Usage visibilityDaily app or text updatesMonthly bill, sometimes with an online portal

Because prepaid plans are usually month-to-month, they can also carry a slightly different rate structure than a 12-month fixed plan from the same provider. Always compare the EFL's average price at the usage level closest to your own home, not just the headline rate. Our guide on how to read an Electricity Facts Label in Texas walks through exactly what to check before you sign up.

Who prepaid electricity actually suits

Prepaid electricity tends to work best for people who want flexibility and control rather than the lowest possible long-term rate. That includes renters who expect to move within a few months, people rebuilding credit, households moving into a new Texas address without proof of an established payment history, and anyone who prefers paying in smaller amounts throughout the month instead of one large bill.

It's less ideal for households on a tight, unpredictable schedule who might miss a low-balance alert, or for anyone who travels frequently and can't check a balance app. If your usage swings wildly with the seasons, see our guide on lowering your electric bill in summer and lowering your electric bill in winter so you're not caught off guard by a bigger daily draw-down.

Pros and cons of prepaid electricity in Texas

Pros:

  • No deposit and usually no credit check to get started
  • Daily visibility into exactly what you're spending
  • Easier to budget in smaller amounts instead of one large monthly bill
  • Often no long-term contract, so you can leave without an early termination fee

Cons:

  • Disconnection can happen quickly once your balance runs out
  • Requires active monitoring, especially during high-usage months
  • Fewer long fixed-rate options compared to postpaid plans
  • Rates can still vary, so you have to compare the EFL carefully rather than assuming prepaid is automatically cheaper

How to switch to, or away from, prepaid electricity

If you're moving to Texas or starting service at a new address, you can shop prepaid and postpaid plans side by side using your ZIP code, since Texas is deregulated outside a few municipal and co-op areas. Check the EFL for each plan's average price at your typical usage level, confirm which Transmission and Distribution Utility (TDU) serves your address, such as Oncor, CenterPoint, AEP Texas, or TNMP, since that delivery charge applies no matter which provider you choose. Our breakdown of Texas TDU delivery charges shows the fixed and per-kWh fees for each utility.

If you already have postpaid service and you're considering a move to prepaid (or the reverse), remember that Texas lets you switch without an early termination fee within 14 days before a fixed contract expires, or when you're moving with proof of a new address. You also get 3 federal business days after signing any new contract to cancel for any reason. For the full process, see our guide on how to switch electricity providers in Texas, and check the best time to switch electricity providers in Texas so you're not caught mid-contract.

What to do next

Start by deciding whether a deposit or a daily balance is the bigger risk for your household. If a deposit is the obstacle, compare prepaid plans and the no-deposit options in our Texas electricity with no deposit guide. If you choose prepaid, set a low-balance alert well above your average daily cost, check your app at least twice a week during extreme weather, and compare the EFL's average price at your real usage level before you commit. You can compare current plans, including prepaid options, for your area using our Texas electricity rates page.
faq: Does prepaid electricity in Texas require a deposit?
No. Most prepaid electricity plans in Texas skip the deposit and credit check entirely, since you're always paying for power before you use it rather than being extended credit.
How fast can prepaid electricity get disconnected?
Disconnection can happen quickly, sometimes the same day your balance hits zero, which is faster than the billing and grace-period process used for postpaid accounts.
Is prepaid electricity cheaper than postpaid in Texas?

Not automatically. Both plan types publish an Electricity Facts Label with average price per kWh at 500, 1,000 and 2,000 kWh, so you need to compare those numbers directly rather than assuming prepaid is cheaper.
Can I switch from prepaid to a regular postpaid plan later?

Yes. You can shop and switch electricity providers in Texas at any time, and you won't pay an early termination fee if you switch within 14 days before a fixed contract ends or when moving with proof of a new address.
